name: Toffee
lede: Toffee is a warm, mid brown named for the boiled-sugar candy, recorded by Werner in 1821 among his examples but never explained there.

sections.title: A candy's brown
sections.body:
Our library records Toffee, #A36629, as a Werner name from 1821; the book gives natural examples for its colors but not a reason for this particular name, so its choice of "toffee" over any other brown is undocumented here [1]. The candy itself, a boiled mix of sugar and butter, was a known English sweet by the early nineteenth century, consistent with the date [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[sudan-brown]], [[ochre-brown]] and [[colour]], at 3.2, 3.4 and 4.2 ΔE [1]. It also shares canvases more than chance would predict with [[chocolate]] and a color called Chamoline [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this brown in 1,391 of 23,781 paintings, 5.85 percent, more common than 88 percent of our named colors, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1300s, in 22 of 251 paintings, 8.8 percent of the paintings we have from that century, over three times the archive's rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 69 percent of its appearances, rather than a shadow or base tone [3]. The earliest dated example in our data is from the year 1000; that is centuries before the word "toffee" itself is recorded, so the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, never a proof of toffee-colored paint, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].

questions.q: True or false: Werner's 1821 book explains why he chose the name Toffee.

openers: Toffee has sat almost exactly on top of a color called Gallstone Yellow in our library the whole time.
